te: Imagine this. It happens to many middle class families in India.
You pay thirty five thousand rupees every year for health insurance. You renew it on time for six straight years. You never miss a single payment.
Then, an emergency. Your father is admitted to the hospital.
Three days later, it is nine o'clock at night. You are standing at the billing counter. The discharge papers are ready. The bill is four and a half lakh rupees.
The man at the desk hands you one printed letter. It says, sorry sir, your cashless request is denied. Reason, non disclosure of a pre existing disease.
Your heart drops. Your family panics.
It is night. The banks are closed. You break your fixed deposit, borrow from relatives, or swipe a credit card, just to take your father home.
And you ask, why did I pay all these years, if they leave me alone the one time I need them?
Here is the truth. In most cases like this, the door is not closed. A cashless denial is not a claim rejection. And after five years of policy, there is a rule that stops this exact excuse.
Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore.
In this video, we will not shout, and we will not sell you any policy. We will read the real IRDAI rules, see who really says no, and learn the step by step way to get your money back.
Let us break it down in simple words.
First, who actually says no to you at the hospital desk?
Most people think the insurance company itself is checking your reports. But usually, the papers go to a middleman called a TPA. Third Party Administrator.
Many think a TPA is a neutral government doctor. It is not. A TPA is a company licensed by IRDAI. The insurance company hires it and pays it, to process your claim papers.
IRDAI even says the TPA's pay cannot depend on how much claim money gets paid out. But here is the part most people never hear.

Under IRDAI rules, no claim can be rejected without the approval of the insurance company's own claims review committee. And if they reject it, fully or partly, they must tell you the exact policy clause.
So, a cashless no at the desk only means one thing. The company did not agree to pay the hospital directly, at that moment. Your right to claim the money is still alive.
Now, three reasons you will often see on these letters.
Reason number one. Non disclosure of a pre existing disease.
Say you were admitted for a broken leg, or dengue. A junior doctor writes one line in your notes. Patient has mild blood pressure.
The reviewer sees that one line. He opens your proposal form from five years ago, and says, you did not declare blood pressure. Cashless denied.
Many families ask, does blood pressure cause a broken leg? It does not. But in the first five years of your policy, the company can still raise this question. After five years, the rule changes.
Reason number two. Not medically necessary. They say your treatment could have been done without staying in hospital.
Reason number three. Room rent limit, and proportionate deduction.
Say your policy allows a room of five thousand rupees a day. But you took a room of eight thousand. They do not just cut the three thousand rupee difference.
They pay only five out of every eight rupees, on the surgery, doctor and nursing charges too. That is a cut of about thirty seven percent on those charges.
One good thing. Many policies do not apply this cut to medicines, and some also leave out implants and tests. Check what your policy wording says, and check your bill.
When a family sees these letters, they feel helpless. They think the door is closed forever.
It is not. Here is the rule that protects you.
Now listen carefully. This may be the most important rule in health insurance.
It is called the moratorium period.
Earlier, this period was eight years. In twenty twenty four, IRDAI brought it down from eight years to five years.
That means sixty months in a row, with no break in your policy.
So what does it mean for you?
After five years of continuous cover, the company cannot question your policy or your claim, saying you did not disclose something, or you gave wrong details.
So after five years, an old health history cannot be called non disclosure.
There is only one exception. Proven fraud. Not a small mistake, not a forgotten fever. Fraud that the company has to establish.

Two honest points. Your normal policy limits and exclusions still apply. And if you change insurer by porting, your years move with you. If you cancel and buy a new policy, the count starts again from zero.
Now think about our family at the billing counter. Six years of policy. A denial letter that says non disclosure. That excuse goes against the IRDAI rule.
And one more rule. A clock.
When you ask for cashless, the company must decide within one hour. And when the hospital sends the discharge request, the company must give final approval within three hours.

IRDAI says the patient should not be made to wait for discharge. If the approval comes later than three hours, any extra amount the hospital charges for that delay is paid by the insurance company, from its own funds, not by you.
So remember this rule, and ask for it at the discharge counter.
So, what should you do if your cashless is denied at the counter tonight?
Do not shout at the hospital staff. Do not panic. Follow these four steps.
Step one. Collect your papers before you leave.
If you have to pay the bill yourself, pay it. But before you leave the hospital, ask for copies of these papers.
The discharge summary. The final bill with full break up. All test reports and pharmacy bills. And the cashless denial letter.
If they said the admission was not needed, ask your treating doctor for a short letter on why it was needed.
Step two. File a reimbursement claim quickly, within the time your policy gives. Some policies give only fifteen days from discharge, some give thirty.

If they reject it, write to the company's grievance officer. Keep it calm and clear. Give your policy number, claim number and amount. If your policy has crossed five years, quote the moratorium rule.
The company has to reply to your complaint within fourteen days.
Step three. Register your complaint on Bima Bharosa.

If the company ignores you, or sends the same reply again, go to bimabharosa dot irdai dot gov dot in. This is IRDAI's own complaint portal. Your complaint goes to the company, and IRDAI can see it and track it.
And step four. The strongest one. The Insurance Ombudsman.
If the company rejects your complaint, or does not reply for thirty days, you do not need a court case or an expensive lawyer.
Go to the Insurance Ombudsman website, cioins dot co dot in.
The Ombudsman system was set up by the government, to settle complaints of policyholders against insurance companies.
You can file the complaint online. It costs nothing. You can explain your case yourself, without a lawyer. File it within one year of the company's final reply.
Now the good part. In the year twenty twenty four, twenty five, the Ombudsman offices received over thirty two thousand health insurance complaints.
Out of the cases they settled or decided, about three out of every four went in favour of the policyholder.
And about eight out of ten complaints were closed within three months.

The Ombudsman can award up to fifty lakh rupees. The award is binding on the insurance company. Unless the company challenges the award, it must pay within thirty days, or pay you a penalty of five thousand rupees for every day of delay.
And if you are not happy with the award, you can still go to a consumer court.
That is how you fight back. Not with anger. With the rules.
Finally, let us be practical. How do you stop this problem before you even reach a hospital?
When you buy or renew health insurance, remember three rules.
Rule one. Never hide anything in the proposal form. Write it down.
If you smoke now and then, if you have mild thyroid or blood pressure, write it clearly in the form.
Yes, the company may charge extra, or add a waiting period. But once it is written in your form, it cannot later call it non disclosure.
Rule two. Look for a policy with no room rent limit, or stay in a room within your limit.
A cheaper policy with a room rent limit of one percent of the cover can look like a saving. But one night in a bigger room can cut a big part of your surgery claim.
Rule three. Ask about a consumables cover.

Gloves, masks, syringes and similar items are often not paid by a normal policy. Reports say they can be five to fifteen percent of a hospital bill. Some insurers sell an add on cover for this. Check the price before you buy.
Remember, you pay for health insurance so your family has peace of mind in its weakest moment.
Do not let a denial letter scare you. Know the five year rule. Use the Ombudsman. And protect your hard earned savings.
Be smart. Be informed. And always, be practical.
